questions.topic: Balanced Search Trees vs Hash Indexes: Range vs Point Lookups
questions.question: What worst-case height does a balanced search tree maintain for n keys?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)

questions.topic: Balanced Search Trees vs Hash Indexes: Range vs Point Lookups
questions.question: Which workload most directly favors a hash index over a balanced tree?
options: Ordered range scans with floor and ceiling queries
Memory-resident exact lookups with no ordering requirement
Prefix enumeration followed by lexicographic output
Worst-case bounded lookup against adversarial collisions

questions.topic: Balanced Search Trees vs Hash Indexes: Range vs Point Lookups
questions.question: What is the balanced-tree cost to return k keys from a range?
options: O(1), because a range is stored in one tree node
O(n), because every tree key must be inspected
O(log n + k), for boundary search plus output traversal
O(k log n), because the root must be revisited for every key

questions.topic: Balanced Search Trees vs Hash Indexes: Range vs Point Lookups
questions.question: Why can inserting sorted keys into an ordinary unbalanced binary search tree be disastrous?
options: The keys collide into one hash bucket and overwrite each other
The tree rotates after every comparison and becomes completely full
The insertion order forces every key into the root node
The tree can become a chain with O(n) lookup and update

questions.topic: Balanced Search Trees vs Hash Indexes: Range vs Point Lookups
questions.question: Why must an ordered index persist its comparator and normalization semantics?
options: Different comparison rules can leave an inserted key unreachable at lookup
The comparator determines how many buckets the index must allocate up front
Normalization holds tree height constant regardless of the stored key count
Persisting the comparison rules removes the need to rebalance on update

questions.topic: Balanced Search Trees vs Hash Indexes: Range vs Point Lookups
questions.question: When is maintaining both a hash index and ordered index defensible?
options: When neither point nor ordered queries occur often enough to measure
When both access paths justify added memory and coordinated update cost
When all data is immutable and no lookup of any kind is required
When duplicate structures are guaranteed to update themselves without coordination

questions.topic: B-tree Intuition: Wide Nodes for Block Storage
questions.question: Why do B-tree nodes contain many keys and child pointers?
options: To maximize binary-tree height and increase page reads
To store every index key in the root page
To gain large branching factor from each expensive page fetch
To replace key ordering with expected constant-time hashing

questions.topic: B-tree Intuition: Wide Nodes for Block Storage
questions.question: Where does a B+ tree normally store row pointers or records?
options: In the root page, and nowhere else
In the internal routing nodes
In a separate unordered hash table
In the leaf pages at the bottom

questions.topic: B-tree Intuition: Wide Nodes for Block Storage
questions.question: A B-tree has an effective fan-out of 256 and indexes about one billion keys. Roughly how many page levels are needed?
options: About four
About sixteen
About thirty
About two hundred fifty-six

questions.topic: B-tree Intuition: Wide Nodes for Block Storage
questions.question: What happens when inserting into a full B-tree leaf?
options: The new key is discarded to preserve page occupancy
The leaf splits and a separator is inserted into its parent
Every leaf is rewritten as an independent binary tree
The root is deleted and replaced by the overflowing leaf

questions.topic: B-tree Intuition: Wide Nodes for Block Storage
questions.question: Why are linked B+ tree leaves valuable for range scans?
options: They scatter each output key onto a randomly chosen storage page
They pin every leaf page in the buffer cache for the whole scan
They let one range scan continue across sequential leaf pages
They drop key ordering so leaves can be written in arrival order

questions.topic: B-tree Intuition: Wide Nodes for Block Storage
questions.question: Why is a B-tree over full document text not a substitute for an inverted index?
options: A B-tree cannot store strings or compare them lexicographically
An inverted index supports only exact whole-document equality
A B-tree always tokenizes every key into term postings automatically
It orders complete keys rather than mapping contained terms to documents

questions.topic: Tries and FSTs for Prefix Lookup and Autocomplete
questions.question: What does a path from a trie root represent?
options: A sequence of symbols spelling a stored prefix
A random hash-probe sequence for one key
A list of page numbers ordered by insertion time
A balanced-tree rotation history for one term

questions.topic: Tries and FSTs for Prefix Lookup and Autocomplete
questions.question: What is the lookup cost for a trie key of length L, assuming efficient edge access?
options: O(L)
O(log L)
O(nL)

questions.topic: Tries and FSTs for Prefix Lookup and Autocomplete
questions.question: How does path compression reduce a naive trie's overhead?
options: It hashes all outgoing edges into one unordered terminal node
It duplicates shared prefixes for every stored completion
It collapses nonbranching symbol chains into multi-symbol edges
It removes terminal markers and makes complete keys indistinguishable

questions.topic: Tries and FSTs for Prefix Lookup and Autocomplete
questions.question: What additional capability turns a finite-state automaton into a transducer?
options: It stores each input key in an independent binary tree
It removes deterministic transitions and accepts random paths
It prevents final states from representing complete terms
It associates outputs with transitions or final states

questions.topic: Tries and FSTs for Prefix Lookup and Autocomplete
questions.question: Why can a minimized FST be smaller than a trie?
options: It can merge equivalent suffix states as well as share prefixes
It stores every term as an uncompressed independent string
It removes all edges needed for prefix enumeration
It allocates one full alphabet pointer array per input symbol

questions.topic: Tries and FSTs for Prefix Lookup and Autocomplete
questions.question: Why are large compact FST dictionaries commonly immutable?
options: They cannot attach a value or a postings offset to a complete term
They share states globally, so one local edit breaks the minimality
They accept only unsorted input and must be rebuilt after every lookup
Their transitions store process addresses that cannot be serialized
